<explanation>
Below is an explanation tailored to drawing an accurate system design diagram for PDF Craft:

1. Project Type & Purpose:
   • PDF Craft is a Python library designed to process scanned PDFs. It converts PDFs into Markdown files or EPUB ebooks by extracting text (using OCR) and analyzing layout/cues from a scanned page.
   • The library integrates AI models – including an OCR engine (OnnxOCR), layout detection (DocLayout-YOLO, layoutreader), and LLM services (DeepSeek) – to produce semantically organized output and correct OCR artifacts.
   • It is used as a processing pipeline that takes in a PDF, passes it through multiple stages (OCR page extraction, content analysis, correction via LLM) and finally outputs text (Markdown or structured EPUB).

2. Analyzing the File Structure:
   • There is a clear project package “pdf_craft” with sub-packages:
     - "analyser": Contains modules such as asset_matcher, chapter, page, state_machine, etc. These indicate that it’s responsible for examining the PDF’s layout/structure (e.g., splitting pages, handling chapters, citations, positions, etc.).
     - "epub": Modules like gen_epub, gen_index, gen_part – these are focused on assembling content into EPUB, managing chapters and the overall ebook structure.
     - "llm": Contains modules for integration with LLM services to analyze and improve OCR output (error.py, executor.py, node.py). The LLM component is intended to refine the text, generate structured information, and adapt the document based on LLM responses.
     - "pdf": Focuses on lower-level PDF operations (document parsing, text matching, sections) – essentially doing the heavy lifting for extracting text blocks from PDF files.
     - Other files like markdown.py and template.py indicate the creation of Markdown output and templating for various target formats.
   • The “data” directory holds Jinja templates and prompt files that enable customization and formatting for both analysis and EPUB generation. The presence of both “prompts” and “templates” means that the design is modular with configurable output formats.
   • The scripts folder contains sample command-line scripts that invoke various functions (analyzing, generating epub/markdown) to demonstrate how the library should be used.
   • Testing modules demonstrate that components such as page clipping and serial extraction have independent tests, which suggests a decoupled design.

3. Key Components & Their Relationships:
   a. Input/Processing:
      – PDF Input: The system takes a PDF file as input.
      – PDF Extractor (located in pdf_craft/pdf and PDFPageExtractor referenced in README): Reads pages and extracts initial text and images.
      – OCR Module: Uses OnnxOCR (and optionally GPU support via CUDA) to recognize text from scanned images.
   b. Analysis:
      – The “analyser” package processes extracted content. It handles tasks such as separating header/footer, matching citations, analyzing page layout, linking content between pages, and extracting chapters.
      – It uses prompt templates (in the “data/prompts” directory) to interact with the LLM.
   c. LLM Integration:
      – The “llm” package acts as an interface between the local extraction/analysis and external LLM services (DeepSeek) for error correction and chapter structuring.
      – It also handles advanced configuration (retries, temperature control).
   d. Output Generators:
      – Markdown Writer: Exports the final content to Markdown (pdf_craft/markdown.py).
      – EPUB Generator: The “epub” package modules generate EPUB files using the analyzed data and templating system.
      – Both generators reference the Jinja templates (in “data/templates”) to consistently format the output.
   e. Auxiliary/Supporting Components:
      – Scripts provide various usage examples.
      – Testing modules ensure quality and proper isolation of functional components.
      – CI/CD configuration files and manifests (.github/workflows, setup.py, etc.) help with building, linting, and deployment.

4. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   • Modularity: Each major function – PDF extraction, analysis, LLM correction, final content generation – is split into its own set of modules and packages.
   • Pipeline Architecture: The data flows from input, through extraction, analysis, correction, and finally into one of the output pathways (Markdown or EPUB).
   • Template Driven: Use of Jinja templates for both prompts and output formatting is a key design decision.
   • Extensibility: The design separates OCR, LLM integration, and output generation, which makes it easier to replace or upgrade individual parts (e.g., switching OCR engines or LLM services).
   • Testability: The clear separation into packages and independent test modules (in “tests”) ensures each component can be developed and verified in isolation.

5. Guidelines to Create the Diagram:
   • Begin by sketching the high-level pipeline:
     - Start with the PDF Input.
     - Draw a block for the PDF Extractor (including OCR module integration).
     - Branch the processing into two parallel analysis paths:
         ◦ One for Markdown conversion (using extraction and direct text assembly).
         ◦ Another that feeds into the LLM — include an “LLM Connector” component.
     - From the LLM branch, show processing through the analyzer (content segmentation, chapter and citation detection).
     - Finally, output blocks: Markdown Writer and EPUB Generator.
   • Detail the internal components:
     - In the “Extraction” block, include sub-components: PDF parser, OCR engine, and image extraction.
     - In the “Analysis” block, include page analysis, state machine for scanning, citation extraction, etc.
     - In the “LLM Integration” block, list configuration parameters (key, model, temperature) and error-handling mechanisms.
     - In the “Output Generation” block, include references to the templating system (Jinja templates for EPUB and Markdown).
   • Include support/auxiliary blocks:
     - Configuration/CI: Represent the GitHub workflows and setup scripts.
     - Testing Environment: A test suite component ensuring quality for each module.
   • Use directional arrows to indicate the flow of data from JavaScript-like “entry” (PDF input) through processing, analysis, and output.
   • Use color coding or different shapes to highlight the distinct layers (e.g., Input Layer, Processing Layer, Analysis Layer, Output Layer, and Integration Services).

6. Visual Elements for the Diagram:
   – Clearly labeled components: “PDF Extractor – OCR”, “Content Analyzer”, “LLM Integration”, “Markdown Writer”, “EPUB Generator”.
   – Directional arrows showing data flow from PDF → Extraction → Analysis (with split paths).
   – Use different shapes: rectangles for processing modules, cylinders for external services (LLM, possibly external OCR if depicted), and databases if you want to illustrate the temporary storage in “analysing_dir_path”.
   – Optionally include icons or annotations for external dependencies (e.g., “OnnxOCR”, “DeepSeek”).

7. Final Advice:
   • Focus on detailing all essential actor modules – don’t hesitate to break down each high-level component into individual functions where necessary.
   • The diagram should enable anyone reviewing it to understand the entire flow from raw PDF input to the generation of a finished Markdown or EPUB file.
   • By keeping the system components granular (extraction modules, analysis modules, templating, and output generators) you can visually represent how data is transformed.
   • Make sure to incorporate configuration and error management flows which are critical in the LLM and OCR modules.

Following these guidelines will give you a comprehensive and accurate architectural diagram that covers PDF Craft’s flux from input to final content generation, ensuring that its modular design, extensibility, and integration points are clear at a glance.
</explanation>
